claude.sample_unit: patients in temporal validation cohort (diagnosed 2005); 4683 in development
models_evaluated: flexible parametric cause-specific survival models (standard approach)

links.outcome: Calibration of 10-year predicted vs observed risk after recalibrating baseline hazard with recent data
links.effect: Standard approach over-estimated 10-year all-cause CIF by 0.028 (95% CI 0.015, 0.041); temporal recalibration 0.013 (0.000, 0.026); period analysis 0.005 (-0.008, 0.018).
links.quote: Using temporal recalibration or period analysis improved the calibration of the predicted risks across the full range of follow‐up, where particular improvements can be seen in the predicted risk of death due to colon cancer and the total risk of death.

links.outcome: Calibration drift from improving survival trends in temporally later patients
links.effect: Standard model over-estimated 10-year risk of colon cancer death by 0.019, other causes 0.008, all causes 0.028 in patients diagnosed 2005.
links.quote: Using the standard approach to develop each model led to an over‐estimation of 0.019, 0.008 and 0.028 for the 10‐year marginal CIFs for colon cancer, other causes and all causes respectively, see Table 4 .

links.outcome: Calibration in patients aged 85+ across recalibration methods
links.effect: For patients aged 85 and over, period analysis under-estimated the CIF whereas temporal recalibration produced better calibrated predictions.
links.quote: Here, it can be seen that using period analysis under‐estimated the CIF whilst using temporal recalibration produced better calibrated risk predictions.

period analysis with delayed entry for model development
extending recalibration to competing risks by recalibrating each cause-specific model separately

models_evaluated: standard cause-specific flexible parametric survival models

links.effect: Standard approach overestimated 10-year marginal CIFs by 0.019 for colon cancer, 0.008 other causes, and 0.028 all causes.
links.quote: Using the standard approach to develop each model led to an over‐estimation of 0.019, 0.008 and 0.028 for the 10‐year marginal CIFs for colon cancer, other causes and all causes respectively, see Table 4 .

links.effect: Standard approach overestimated 10-year CIFs: colon 0.019 [0.007, 0.032], other 0.008 [−0.004, 0.020], all causes 0.028 [0.015, 0.041].
links.quote: Using the standard approach to develop each model led to an over‐estimation of 0.019, 0.008 and 0.028 for the 10‐year marginal CIFs for colon cancer, other causes and all causes respectively, see Table 4 .

links.effect: At 10 years, all-cause overestimation dropped from 0.028 [0.015, 0.041] to 0.013 [0.000, 0.026]; period analysis to 0.005 [−0.008, 0.018].
links.quote: Using temporal recalibration or period analysis improved the calibration of the predicted risks across the full range of follow‐up, where particular improvements can be seen in the predicted risk of death due to colon cancer and the total risk of death.

unlisted_practices: Period analysis using delayed entry and recent period windows for prognostic model development

links.outcome: 10-year calibration of cause-specific and all-cause mortality risk predictions
links.effect: Standard approach overestimated 10-year CIF by 0.019 (colon cancer) and 0.028 (all causes); temporal recalibration reduced differences to 0.007 and 0.013, respectively.
links.quote: The 10-year calibration plots demonstrated that using the standard approach over-estimated the risk of death due to colon cancer and the total risk of death and that calibration was improved using temporal recalibration or period analysis.

unlisted_practices: period analysis using delayed entry to account for survival trends in risk prediction models
temporal recalibration of cause-specific hazard models in competing risk settings
